title: TradeReady: importing into and exporting from Australia (customs, biosecurity, regulated goods, export controls)
notes: First sourced rules for TradeReady. Built from Australian Border Force, Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, ATO, TGA, Department of Defence, business.gov.au and ABLIS pages read on 2026-10-10. Every reference is UNVERIFIED and carries a summary, not the source's wording: staff must capture each source, replace the extract with the exact text and verify it. The Customs Act 1901, the Customs (Prohibited Imports) and (Prohibited Exports) Regulations, the Biosecurity Act 2015 and the Export Control Act 2020 are not encoded.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Goods valued above A$1,000 that arrive by mail, air cargo or sea cargo generally need an import declaration to clear them from customs control. The importer can lodge it electronically in the Integrated Cargo System (ICS), which needs a digital certificate and client registration in the ICS, or a licensed customs broker can lodge it. The declaration is used to assess duty, GST and other taxes and charges. Records must be kept for five years.
references.interpretation: Above A$1,000 a full import declaration is generally required; it can be lodged by the importer (after ICS client registration) or by a licensed customs broker. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Licensed customs brokers clear imported goods for importers: they lodge import declarations in the ICS, classify goods under the Customs Tariff to work out duty and tax, and make sure regulated goods such as motor vehicles and firearms meet government requirements before release. Import declarations may be lodged by the importer or by a licensed broker.
references.interpretation: Using a broker is optional but common; brokers also check regulated goods such as vehicles and firearms. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] The Australian Government restricts some goods from being brought into or sent out of Australia. Most prohibited goods can be imported or exported with written permission if conditions are met; some are absolutely prohibited. Tobacco needs permission to import and all duties and taxes must be paid when it arrives. Importing or exporting without permission can lead to seizure, penalties of up to 2,500 penalty units, up to 10 years' imprisonment, or both. The importer or exporter must confirm the goods can be brought in or taken out.
references.interpretation: Restricted goods (including tobacco) need written permission before import. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Most goods valued up to A$1,000 can be imported without a formal import declaration. Goods over A$1,000, prohibited or restricted goods, biosecurity risks and goods that attract duty involve more reporting. You must declare all goods arriving in Australia unless an exception applies. A licensed customs broker can handle the importation. Most imports attract 10% GST, and some also attract customs duty, processing charges, dumping duties, and brokerage, permit and biosecurity fees. Commercial imports of industrial chemicals, or of products containing them such as soap, paint or glue, need registration with the Australian Industrial Chemicals Introduction Scheme (AICIS), which has an annual fee. A logistics provider handles transport, storage and handling.
references.interpretation: General importing obligations, AICIS registration for chemicals and the role of brokers and logistics providers. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Goods worth more than A$2,000 generally need an export declaration before they leave Australia. Some goods can't be exported without a permit. The Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry controls the export of some agricultural products. Austrade's Export Market Development Grants help businesses grow their exports.
references.interpretation: Above A$2,000 an export declaration is generally required; permits for some goods apply at any value. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] BICON shows whether a commodity can be imported into Australia, the conditions, documents, treatments and whether a biosecurity import permit is needed. Goods that need a permit but arrive without one are not cleared: they are exported or destroyed. Standard permits are usually issued within 20 business days and non-standard ones within 40 business days. Imported food must also meet Australian food standards and may be referred to the Imported Food Inspection Scheme.
references.interpretation: Food, plant and animal goods must be checked in BICON; some need a permit before they arrive. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Imported food for sale is inspected and tested under the Imported Food Inspection Scheme. Risk food (listed in the Imported Food Control Order 2019) is referred at 100% until a record of passes reduces the rate; surveillance food is referred at random (5%). Food that fails cannot be released and must be relabelled, destroyed or re-exported.
references.interpretation: Food imported for sale can be referred for inspection; risk food always is at first. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] From 1 September to 30 April, target high risk goods (tariff chapters 44, 45, 57, 68-70, 72-76, 78-89, which include timber, stone, ceramics, glass, metals, machinery, electrical equipment and vehicles) made in or shipped from target risk countries (much of Europe, Russia, Türkiye, parts of Central Asia, the United States and Canada) need mandatory treatment. Break bulk, open top and flat rack cargo must be treated offshore; untreated break bulk is directed for export. Containers can be treated onshore, which may delay clearance.
references.interpretation: Seasonal stink bug treatment applies to some goods by sea from listed countries. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] The department controls exports of prescribed goods: dairy, eggs, fish, live animals, meat, poultry, rabbit and ratite meat, wild game, organic products, plants and wood. Premises that prepare or store prescribed goods for export must be registered establishments under the Export Control Act 2020, applied for through the Export Service. Importing-country requirements are in the Manual of Importing Country Requirements (MICoR), and registered exporters get certificates through EXDOC.
references.interpretation: Exporting prescribed agricultural goods needs a registered establishment and government export documents. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.section: Approval to import and supply a vehicle
references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Anyone bringing a new or second-hand road vehicle into Australia needs an approval, which must be obtained before the vehicle is imported. Approval is also needed to supply the vehicle in the Australian market. Some exemptions exist, such as for vehicles made before 1 January 1989. The Department of Infrastructure administers it.
references.interpretation: A vehicle import approval must be in place before the vehicle is shipped. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] To import, manufacture or sell in-scope electrical equipment you must be registered as a responsible supplier. Equipment is in scope if it is rated above 50 V AC (or 120 V ripple-free DC), below 1000 V AC (or 1500 V DC), and designed or marketed for household, personal or similar use. Equipment falls into three risk levels with different registration and certification requirements.
references.interpretation: Importers of household mains-powered electrical equipment must register as a responsible supplier. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] A licence is needed to import equipment containing ozone depleting substances or synthetic greenhouse gases, such as refrigeration or air-conditioning units using HFC or HCFC refrigerants, including where the system is built into a vehicle, boat, caravan, machine, refrigerator or water cooler. It is not needed for a consignment of no more than five pieces of equipment totalling less than 10 kg.
references.interpretation: Importing refrigerant-charged equipment above the small-consignment exemption needs a licence. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] A permit is needed to import CITES-listed species, and products from them, and to export Australian native plants and animals or products from threatened native species. The National Environmental Protection Agency administers it.
references.interpretation: Trade in CITES species and native wildlife needs a wildlife trade permit. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Eligible importers can defer GST on taxable imports and pay it in their monthly business activity statement instead of at the border. They need an ABN, GST registration, monthly BAS lodged online and paid electronically, and up-to-date tax affairs.
references.interpretation: GST-registered importers who lodge monthly may defer import GST. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] Medical devices generally must be included in the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods (ARTG) before they can be supplied in Australia, unless an exemption applies. Each ARTG entry is specific to the sponsor, so an importer must apply even if another sponsor has an entry for the same device. Sponsors keep records, report adverse events and run recalls.
references.interpretation: Therapeutic goods imported for supply generally need their own ARTG entry. Captured on 2026-10-10 from a reading of the published page; the exact wording was not copied. Replace this with the source's own text, capture a snapshot and verify before relying on it.

references.extracted_text: [Summary, not the source's wording] A permit is needed to export or supply goods, software or technology on the Defence and Strategic Goods List, including dual-use items, and to supply listed technology to a foreign person in Australia. Firearms, parts, accessories and ammunition always need a permit before export. Applications go through the My Australian Defence Export (MADE) portal.

rule_sets.title: Australia: clearing imports through customs
rule_sets.description: Import declarations, ICS registration, GST and duty, and help with freight, from Australian Border Force, ATO and business.gov.au guidance.
limitations: Built from Australian Border Force, ATO and business.gov.au guidance, not from the Customs Act 1901 or its regulations.
Doesn't classify your goods or work out duty rates, free trade agreement rates, tariff concessions or anti-dumping duty.
Uses the value of a typical shipment; each consignment is assessed on its own value.
Not customs or tax advice. Check with a licensed customs broker or the Australian Border Force.

rules.title: Import declaration

outcomes.title: A full import declaration is generally not needed
